Facebook Official
FAYS-book uh-FISH-ul
adjective (Millennial slang)
From Facebook (launched 2004; open to the public 2006), whose profile let users list a "relationship status" ("In a relationship with …", "Engaged", "It’s complicated"). By about 2007 a couple was Facebook official (abbreviated FBO) when both had publicly linked their profiles, which became, for many Millennials, the moment a relationship was considered real. The phrase spread to anything publicly announced ("it’s not official until it’s on Facebook").

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To be Facebook official is to have declared your relationship publicly on your profile: "In a relationship with …" For Millennials it was a milestone, sometimes more significant than meeting the parents. The Christian observation: there is something right in the instinct. A relationship that matters ought to be public. Scripture makes the public declaration central to marriage: Boaz took ten elders of the city and said to them and all the people, "Ye are witnesses this day" (Rut 4:9); the covenant is made before God and witnesses, and "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder" (Mat 19:6). Secret relationships, hidden from family and church, are usually unhealthy ones. But "Facebook official" shows what happened when the public declaration lost its covenant. The status could be changed with a click, announced and withdrawn a dozen times, and the audience was a crowd of acquaintances rather than witnesses with any authority or responsibility. It made relationships performative and their endings public humiliations. Biblical publicity is accountable: the families know, the church knows, and the promises are vows. A father tells his son: do not hide a relationship from me, from your church, or from her father; and do not perform one for the internet either. The only relationship status that means something is the one made before God, with witnesses who will hold you to it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial slang (c. 2007, from Facebook relationship status) for publicly declaring a relationship online; right in wanting publicity, wrong in replacing accountable witnesses and vows with a revocable status (Rut 4:9; Mat 19:6).

expand to see more

FACEBOOK OFFICIAL, adj. (Millennial slang, c. 2007–2010s; abbrev. FBO) Of a romantic relationship, publicly declared via linked Facebook relationship statuses; by extension, formally announced.

Webster (1828), root official: OFFICIAL, adjective 1. Pertaining to an office or public trust. The secretary is engaged in official duties. 2. Derived from the proper office or officer, or from the proper authority; made or communicated by virtue of authority; as an official statement or report. We have official intelligence of the battle. 3. Conducive by virtue of appropriate powers. The stomach and other parts official to nutrition. [Unusual.]

Decode for parents: ask who actually knows about your child’s relationship; family and church witnesses matter more than followers.

Key Scripture

Rut 4:9 — "And Boaz said unto the elders, and unto all the people, Ye are witnesses this day, that I have bought all that was Elimelech's, and all that was Chilion's and Mahlon's, of the hand of Naomi."

Mat 19:6 — "Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

Pro 18:22 — "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD."

Ecc 5:4-5 — "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay."

Heb 13:4 — "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge."

Modern Corruption

Facebook official made a relationship public without making it accountable; Scripture’s publicity is a covenant made before God and witnesses.

expand to see more

The corruption is publicity without covenant. The online status offered the feeling of commitment with none of its substance: no vow, no witnesses with standing, no families joined, and an exit button always visible. Relationships became performances for an audience, and their endings, "single," "it’s complicated," became public spectacles. It trained a generation to treat declarations as provisional.

The recovery is the accountable promise. "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it … Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay" (Ecc 5:4-5). Teach the young that relationships should be known to those who love them and can counsel them, that serious courtship involves families, and that the only status worth announcing is a vow kept before God. "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD" (Pro 18:22).
